opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. What excites me is that it gets at something robotics has struggled with for decades: the gap between seeing and doing.

Vision and language models have made remarkable progress. You can show a system a picture of a cluttered kitchen counter and it can tell you, quite fluently, what's there and even suggest what to do. But when a robot actually reaches in to pick up a wet glass or fold a towel, all that fluency runs into physics. Friction, deformation, slippage, tiny variations in contact: these things are very hard to infer from pixels alone. I sometimes call this the gap between knowing "what" and knowing "how."

Tactile sensing is one way to close that gap. Humans rely on touch constantly without noticing. Try buttoning a shirt with numb fingers and you realize how much your hands are telling you. If we can give robots rich touch signals and then learn joint representations where vision, language, and touch inform each other, a few exciting things become possible. Language can specify the goal, like "gently pick up the ripe one." Vision can localize it. Touch can verify and correct in real time: is it slipping, is it too soft, did I actually get it?

The other piece I find promising is data. One of the big bottlenecks in robot learning is that we don't have an internet-scale corpus of physical interaction the way we have text and images. Multimodal approaches let us borrow structure from the abundant modalities and ground it with the scarce ones. That doesn't eliminate the data problem, but it may make each hour of real-world robot experience much more valuable.

I want to be careful not to overhype it, though. There's a tendency right now to assume that because language models scaled so impressively, robots will follow the same curve shortly. I'm skeptical of that timeline. Manipulation in unstructured environments is genuinely hard, and I think progress will come from combining learning with good old-fashioned engineering: physics models, clever hardware, careful benchmarks. Multimodal learning is a powerful ingredient, not a magic wand.

But the direction is right. Robots that can see, understand what we ask, and feel what they're doing are much more likely to be reliable and safe partners. That's what gets me out of bed in the morning.

r001.rationale: The response says touch can help a robot verify and correct actions, but does not say a model can describe tactile sensations in words.

r002.rationale: The response does not say a model can generate an image from tactile sensor data.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, what excites me most is that for a long time robotics was almost entirely about vision. We had cameras, we had depth sensors, and we got very good at recognizing objects and estimating poses. But when you actually try to pick something up, vision alone tells you remarkably little about what happens at the moment of contact. Is the object slipping? Is it heavier than it looked? Is it soft, is it rigid, is it going to crumple? Humans resolve all of that through touch, almost unconsciously. If you numb someone's fingertips, they struggle to button a shirt even though their eyes work perfectly.

So the exciting thing about bringing tactile sensing into these multimodal models is that we're finally giving robots access to the channel that actually matters for manipulation. And language is the glue. When you can say to a system "pick up the ripe peach but don't bruise it," that instruction has a visual component, finding the peach, and a tactile component, modulating grip force based on how the fruit yields under your fingers. Language lets you connect those two worlds in a way that's natural for people to specify.

I'd add a word of caution, though, because I'm a bit of a skeptic about the hype. Tactile data is much harder to collect at scale than images or text. There's no internet of touch. Every tactile sensor is a little different, they wear out, they drift. So a lot of the hard work ahead is figuring out how to get enough grounded, physical data, through simulation, through careful real-world collection, through clever ways of transferring between sensors. But if we can crack that, I think we'll see robots doing things in homes and hospitals and warehouses that have been stubbornly out of reach for decades. That's what gets me up in the morning.

r001.rationale: The response says language connects visual and tactile information for instructions, but does not say the model can describe in words what a tactile sensor is feeling.

r002.rationale: The response discusses tactile sensing for manipulation, but does not say the model can generate an image consistent with tactile sensor data.

astra-6.text:
What excites me is that these different senses can complement each other. Vision gives you a sense of where an object is and what its shape might be. Language lets you draw on descriptions and communicate what you want the robot to do. But touch tells you something that’s often very hard to see: Have I actually made contact? Is the object slipping? Is it softer than I expected?

Imagine picking up a strawberry. Recognising it is only part of the problem. You also have to figure out how to grasp it firmly enough to lift it without crushing it. And you need to adjust as you go.

The possibility is that we can build systems that connect those observations through action. The robot sees something, makes a prediction, touches it, and revises that prediction. That’s a much richer kind of learning than recognising objects in images. There are still difficult questions about how to combine these signals reliably, but that connection between perception and physical interaction is what I find exciting.

r001.rationale: The response says language can provide descriptions and help communicate what the robot should do, but does not say the model can put what a tactile sensor feels into words.

r002.rationale: The response describes visual and tactile observations informing predictions, but does not say the model can generate an image consistent with tactile data.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me is that these different senses can compensate for one another. Vision gives you a lot of information, but it doesn’t tell you everything you need to know to manipulate an object. You can look at a cup and estimate its shape, but when you grasp it, touch tells you whether it’s slipping, whether it’s heavier than you expected, or whether you’re squeezing too hard.

Language adds another dimension: it lets us communicate goals and draw on descriptions of how things work. The interesting challenge is grounding those descriptions in physical experience. What does “gently” actually mean when you’re picking up a strawberry?

If we can get those sources of information working together, robots could become much better at dealing with unfamiliar objects and recovering when something unexpected happens. That connection between perception and action is what I find especially exciting.
